name: Radical Centrism
summary: Radical centrism is a pragmatic reform outlook that claims to be radical about institutional change and centrist about method, borrowing market tools from the right and social goals from the left. Its adherents favor regulated markets, fiscal responsibility, school choice, universal coverage built on private insurance, need-based rather than race-based preferences, and electoral reforms that loosen two-party dominance. It accepts capitalism and representative democracy and describes itself as idealism without illusions.
scope: The 2000s North American strand set out by Ted Halstead and Michael Lind (The Radical Center, 2001, New America) and by Mark Satin (Radical Middle, 2004, and the Radical Middle Newsletter, 1999-2009), as presented in the New America summary, the American Prospect review of Halstead and Lind, Satin's manifesto and his newsletter articles. It excludes the Third Way of Blair and Giddens, which many radical centrists reject, the personal politics of individual figures such as Lind's restrictionism, and leaders such as Macron. The newsletter often reports other people's proposals (campaign finance, security measures, religion and politics); those answer a statement only where Satin presents them as the radical middle's own. Many statements are unaddressed, so they are null.

missingStatements.text: Every citizen should be required to perform a period of national service.
missingStatements.rationale: Satin's manifesto endorses universal national service as a civic duty.

missingStatements.text: Every child should receive a publicly funded savings account to build assets by adulthood.
missingStatements.rationale: Halstead and Lind propose a nest egg at birth and the manifesto proposes development accounts for poor children.
missingStatements.declined: Narrow policy detail (child savings accounts); not worth a permanent statement every audit must answer.

missingStatements.text: Elections should use ranked-choice voting so that voters can rank candidates in order of preference.
missingStatements.rationale: Halstead and Lind propose rank-ordered voting and Wikipedia lists instant-runoff voting among radical centrist reforms.
missingStatements.declined: Narrow electoral-mechanism detail; proportional-representation partly covers electoral reform and a new statement would burden every audit.

notes: Later pass 2026-11-12 under rules 7: every earlier answer was rechecked. Deductions from the movement's general acceptance of capitalism and representative democracy, answers resting only on Wikipedia, and zeros without a documented split were nulled (67 nullings, each kept in reviewHistory). New sources: 36 pages of Satin's Radical Middle Newsletter and site, saved under scratchpad/sources/radical-centrism/, searched for each theme: economy (health, pensions, anti-poverty, wealth sharing, globalization, trade), government (law reform, campaign finance, global governance), society (affirmative action, feminism, religion, children), world (intervention, terrorism, foreign policy), ecology (energy, nature) and technology (biotech). Most of the newsletter reports other people's ideas, so only positions Satin states as the radical middle's own were counted. The Halstead and Lind book is known only through the New America summary and the Kahlenberg review. Strands differ: Lind favors immigration restriction and economic nationalism, while Satin's manifesto supports free trade with a conscience.
